answers.answer: An embedded database engine runs in the application's process. The application calls SQLite directly to execute SQL rather than sending queries across a boundary to a separate database server; a persistent SQLite database lives in a local file, with in-memory databases also available. Embedded does not remove tables, joins, indexes or transactions. An application-local dataset fits direct local access and avoids a database service; even web users can reach an application server that owns its local SQLite database. Many application servers updating shared data over a network create a harder access pattern: writers must take turns, WAL requires the same machine, and independent copies need extra synchronization software. A client/server database is often a better fit. User count or size alone does not describe writer competition, transaction duration or query cost; workload and access patterns determine fit. An SQLite file does not automatically synchronize devices or resolve conflicting edits.

evidence.quote: The engine runs inside your application's process. Your code calls SQLite directly, rather than sending queries to a separate database server.
A persistent database lives in a local file. SQLite also supports in-memory databases.
SQLite stores data in tables and supports SQL queries, joins, indexes, and transactions.
Sharing changes between independent device or server copies requires additional software. Local transactions do not resolve conflicting edits elsewhere.
Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns.

answers.answer: Affinity guides value conversions in ordinary tables, but each value has a storage class: an integer column can retain unconvertible text. STRICT tables require values to fit their declared type after permitted conversions, except ANY columns. Primary keys identify rows; UNIQUE restricts duplicates; NOT NULL rejects missing values; CHECK rejects false conditions. Required values need explicit NOT NULL because CHECK alone does not make missing values invalid. Foreign keys constrain references to existing rows but permit null unless separately forbidden. Before a transaction, enable PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on every connection and query PRAGMA foreign_keys to verify 1. Atomicity means all grouped changes succeed or none take effect; consistency preserves defined rules; isolation controls concurrent visibility and write coordination, normally hiding incomplete changes; durability means committed changes survive failures within configured guarantees. Commit accepts work and rollback cancels it, preventing a partly accepted group under atomicity. Constraints define the rules consistency can preserve, and correct transaction logic is still necessary because isolation does not remove races or lock waits. A rollback journal records original data for undo, whereas WAL records changes separately. Durability depends on settings, reliable locking and storage honoring flushes; delayed flushing can lose recent committed transactions after power failure. A rollback only covers database work inside the transaction and cannot reverse an external network action.

evidence.quote: A declared integer column can retain text that cannot be converted.
Values must fit the declared type after permitted conversions, except columns explicitly declared ANY.
Combine CHECK with NOT NULL when a missing value must also be invalid.
Before starting a transaction, enable enforcement on each connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, then query PRAGMA foreign_keys and check that it returns 1.
All changes succeed together, or none take effect.
Normal settings hide incomplete changes, but do not remove application races, lock waits or the need for correct transaction logic.
This also requires reliable filesystem locking and storage that honors requests to flush data to persistent media.
Rollback does not reverse an external network side effect.

answers.answer: Several connections, including separate processes on the same machine, may access a database, but only one can actively write that database at a time. Write contention is competition for that required write access. SQLITE_BUSY reports inability to obtain required access. Short write transactions reduce how long others wait; avoid holding a write transaction through network requests. A busy timeout or bounded retries tolerate brief contention, but failed attempts must be handled and some require retrying the transaction. Waiting adds neither another writer nor a success guarantee. Rollback-journal mode saves original data for undo and readers and writers can block each other. WAL writes changes to a separate log, allowing readers to keep a stable snapshot while a writer commits. A checkpoint transfers logged changes into the main database. Long reads can delay checkpoint progress and grow the WAL. WAL still permits only one writer, and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine. Access must respect local-file permissions and reliable filesystem locking; the lesson does not give a complete shared-filesystem compatibility checklist, so those operational details remain to verify rather than assuming a cross-machine shared file works.

evidence.quote: But each database allows only one active writer at a time.
A busy timeout or bounded retry can tolerate brief contention; some failures require retrying the transaction.
A transaction that waits on a network request can hold up unrelated writes.
In this mode, readers and writers can block each other.
Readers can continue using a stable snapshot while a writer commits changes.
Transfers logged changes into the main database file. Long-running reads can delay checkpoint progress and allow the log to grow.
WAL still allows only one writer, and its shared-memory design requires processes on the same machine.

answers.answer: An index is an additional structure that may avoid scanning or sorting all rows; a query plan is the chosen access and processing steps for joins, filters, sorting and aggregation. For a frequent owner-filtered, time-ordered query, a candidate is a composite index with owner then time, matching the filter and requested order. Inspect EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for the chosen access and processing steps, then measure representative queries rather than assuming the index will be used or beneficial. A scan may be preferable for a small table or a query covering much of it. Indexes consume space and require write maintenance; local queries still consume CPU, storage I/O and memory. Without a separate server, the application and host still manage permissions, capacity, recovery and migrations. Coordinate schema changes with application versions and active access; some require rebuilding and copying a table. Retain consistent backups for recovery needs and test restoration and application usability. During WAL activity, committed changes can remain in the log, so the main file alone may omit required state. A supported consistent backup method addresses that consistency requirement. The lesson does not specify how to establish a verified quiescent state or when a plain file copy is sufficient; mere absence of current writes does not establish from this lesson that all needed state is in the main file. Having a backup file alone proves neither correct recovery nor recovery time.

evidence.quote: Chooses access and processing steps for joins, filtering, sorting and aggregation. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows those steps.
Match columns and their order to actual filters and requested ordering; a composite index contains multiple columns.
A scan can be preferable for small tables or broad queries.
Indexes take space and add write maintenance; avoiding a network call does not make expensive work free.
Coordinate it with application versions and active access; some changes require rebuilding a table and copying data.
Use a supported consistent backup method for an active database. Committed data may still be in the WAL, so copying only the main file can omit required state.
A backup file alone does not prove consistency or recovery time.

answers.answer: SQLite is a plausible choice for a single-host application with short occasional writes: data stays close to code, there is no separate database service, and limited write competition may suit one writer at a time. WAL can help readers overlap that writer, but cannot increase simultaneous writers. Several application servers making sustained concurrent writes to shared data suggest choosing a client/server database: independent machines need shared access, competing writes may not be able to take turns, and WAL requires the same machine. Independent SQLite copies would instead need additional synchronization and conflict handling. In either evaluation, define constraints explicitly, verify foreign-key enforcement per connection, choose appropriate typing rules, and use correct transactions. Measure representative query plans and candidate indexes, including write maintenance costs. Use consistent backups and test restoration; a local file does not remove recovery responsibility. Before committing, verify where data resides and which processes/machines access it, actual write contention and transaction durations, failed/busy attempts and acceptable waits, query workload and resource costs, long-reader effects on checkpoints and WAL size, filesystem locking and flush behavior, durability settings, permissions and free space, migration/version requirements, synchronization/conflict needs, and recovery needs plus tested recovery time. The lesson supplies no numerical capacity thresholds or workload measurements, so these choices remain conditional on observed behavior and requirements.

evidence.quote: The key questions are where the data lives and how much work competes to write it.
Measure write contention and transaction duration, not just the number of users.
WAL improves reader/writer overlap; it does not enable simultaneous writers.
The planner need not use an index merely because it exists. Measure representative queries.
Retain backups according to recovery needs, then test restoration and application usability.
Often a better fit when many machines need shared database access or competing writes cannot take turns.
Explain where the data lives, who writes it, and how failures are handled.
